title: Cedi seen easing next week, Kenya shilling up
text:
NAIROBI, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Ghana's cedi and Nigeria's naira are likely to ease slightly next week, while Kenya's shilling should strengthen due to the start of regular year-end dollar inflows.

GHANA

The cedi <GHS=> is seen easing next week, mainly due to growing corporate demand for the dollar. It closed on Wednesday at 1.4265 to the dollar, easing from the week's support around 1.42.

"We expect the coming week's price action to be choppy with potential for the dollar to break higher," said Jacob Brobbey of Barclays Bank said.

Biggles Amponsah of Access Bank Ghana said the cedi could settle at around 1.4300 by the middle of next week.

"Next week may not be so favourable for the cedi, owing to growing demand for dollars, ....notably from the oil and gas sector," he said.

Ghana is on track to become a commercial oil producer by the end of this year. Amponsah said he expected any much further weakening of the cedi to trigger central bank intervention.

NIGERIA

The naira <NGN=D1> is likely to ease further next week, shrugging off central bank attempts to support the currency and calm the forex market by providing a platform for foreign exchange forwards.

"There is still much uncertainty in the market, and most importers are buying up dollars to ... hedge against future depreciation of the naira," one dealer said.

The local currency was trading at 152.36 to the dollar at 1204 GMT, firming slightly from its 152.47 close on Wednesday. State energy firm NNPC sold about $250 million to banks on Tuesday, some of which were delivered on Thursday.

KENYA

Kenya's shilling <KES=> is expected to strengthen against the dollar as traditional year-end inflows from the tourism, tea, coffee and horticulture sectors get under way. A strengthening euro would also underpin the local currency.

Commercial banks posted the shilling at 80.40/50 compared to last Thursday's close of 80.55/65.

Technical analysis showed support for the dollar at 80.15/20, analysts said. The shilling fell through 80.00 on Aug 12 when it closed at 80.25, a level it has not touched since then.

"If the euro continues to gain then we should see the shilling track it," said Kennedy Butiko, deputy head of treasury at Bank of Africa.

TANZANIA

Tanzania's shilling <TZS=> is likely to remain under pressure because of strong corporate dollar demand.

On Wednesday, commercial banks posted the currency at 1,500/1,505 compared with 1,485/1,490 last Thursday.

Traders predicted the shilling would trade in the 1,490-1,500 range in the coming days.

"Overall, we expect the weak shilling to remain at current levels," said Eric Chijoriga, a trader at National Bank of Commerce.

The central Bank of Tanzania traded $62.16 million on its Interbank Foreign Exchange Market in the week ended Tuesday, according to statistics on its website.

UGANDA

The Ugandan shilling <UGX=> is seen in a tight range against the dollar, with a slight weakening bias due to anticipated dollar demand from the energy sector, traders said.

Commercial banks posted the unit at 2,259/2,262 compared with last Thursday's close of 2,247/2,252.

"We expect demand to pick up next week from the energy sector so we are likely to see some slight depreciation of the shilling. We should see trade in the 2,250-2,265 range," said Faisal Bukenya, head of market-making at Barclays Uganda.

Currency traders on Monday agreed to reduce spreads from 10 shillings to 5 shillings because of market illiquidity.

"Interbank activity has picked up given the narrowing of the spreads, although real demand is still absent," Bukenya said.

Charts suggest dollar resistance around 2,275.

"It looks like demand for dollars is building up. We might see a stable shilling next week with demand and supply for dollars evenly matched" said Lucas Ochieng head of treasury at Orient bank.

title: More turbulence in store for African  currencies
text:
*** Reuters has launched a new weekly report looking at short-term prospects for six African currencies, expanding its East African currency report to incorporate a weekly outlook for Nigeria, Zambia and Ghana.

NAIROBI, May 20 (Reuters) - International investor aversion to emerging market assets is likely to weigh on African currencies next week, though some may start to rebound after several days of heavy selling.

KENYA

The shilling <KES=> fell heavily this week, breaking the 79.00 mark against the dollar for the first time in more than a year on the back of continued concerns about the performance of the euro. It may hit 80.00 before starting to recoup losses.

"The euro woes are still bearing heavily on the performance of the shilling," said Chris Muiga, senior trader at Kenya Commercial Bank.

"It seems like we are headed towards 80. I think the next level is a taste of 80 before we see a reversal," said Solomon Alubala, trader at Co-operative Bank.

On Thursday, commercial banks were quoting the shilling at 79.10/20 compared to a Wednesday close of 79.15. It last traded at these levels in late April 2009.

UGANDA

Uganda's shilling <UGX=> hit a seven-month low this week due to concerns emanating from the euro zone, and demand for dollars from the energy sector.

The unit is expected to trade in a 2,180-2,200 range against the dollar over coming days, after closing at 2,215 on Wednesday. The previous Wednesday's close was 2,150.

"We may continue to see a weaker shilling though we expect some correction in the rates in the coming week as corporate demand eases next week," said Faisal Bukenya, head of market making at Barclays Bank Uganda.

Other traders said scant dollar flows into the market would continue to undermine the currency.

"The shilling is likely to shed more value in the days ahead. We anticipate a pick-up in corporate demand towards the end of the month," said another trader at a commercial bank.

Traders are also watching for Central bank intervention.

NIGERIA

The naira <NGN=D1> may buck the trend and firm against the dollar as traders anticipate huge dollar inflows from energy companies, including state oil firm NNPC.

It was trading at 151.77 to the dollar on Thursday, compared to 151.05 on Wednesday.

"We are anticipating month-end dollar sales by some energy companies, including NNPC, by next week which could ease pressure on demand," one dealer said.

Dealers said dollar demand remained strong.

GHANA

The cedi is seen trading in a narrow band of $1.41-$1.42 next week as the market focuses on prospects of oil revenues in late-2010 or early next year.

"That tends to offset the fundamentals," Samir Gadio of Rencap Securities said of expectations of revenues from the Jubilee oilfield, noting that otherwise Ghana would continue to run a relatively high current account deficit.

That deficit stood at around 8 percent of output by the end of 2009 but analysts say strong gold and cocoa prices and the impact of lower imports could help bring it down in 2010.

Sampson Akligoh of Accra-based Databank also saw the cedi underpinned in the medium-term and forecast a 1.5 percent appreciation against the dollar over the course of 2010.

Akligoh said that despite recent central bank moves to cut the prime rate to 15 percent, the yield on the three-year bond available to foreign investors remained sufficiently attractive to keep portfolio inflows buoyant.

ZAMBIA

The kwacha <ZMK=> is likely to strengthen after two weeks of foreigners dumping local treasury bills and buying dollars.

"We expect the kwacha to appreciate to around 4,900 in the coming week mainly because of profit taking ... after (the dollar) breached the psychological mark of 5,000," Finance Bank treasurer Miles Sampa said.

The unit, which tends to track world copper prices because of Zambia's heavy reliance on copper exports, hit 5,130 on May 7 after lurching outside a 4,600-4,700 trading range that has prevailed for most of the previous eight months.

TANZANIA

Commercial banks quoted the shilling <TZS=> at 1,440/1,448 on Thursday, compared with 1,420 at Wednesday's close after a turbulent trading session in which the unit fell as low as 1,470. Last Wednesday's close was 1,406/1,415.

Traders said the shilling could weaken further due to tight dollar supply, predicting a 1,470-1,500 range in the coming days.

"The shilling might depreciate even further next month with the absence of inflows from agriculture. The central bank has not been intervening aggressively in the market," said Esther Manase, a trader at Standard Chartered Bank Tanzania.

Between last Wednesday and Tuesday, the central Bank of Tanzania traded $17 million on its Interbank Foreign Exchange Market, according to statistics on its website.

title: UPDATE 2-Nigerian naira dips to 130 vs dlr as cbank  intervenes
text:
(Adds details, background)

LAGOS, Dec 5 (Reuters) - Nigeria's central bank sold $900 million to retail banks on Friday at its second intervention on the interbank foreign exchange market this week, allowing the naira to depreciate further against the U.S dollar.

Economists say it is in Nigeria's interests for the local currency to fall as the world's eighth-biggest oil exporter tries to mitigate the effects of lower global demand for crude, which is eating into its foreign earnings.

A weaker naira gives the government greater spending power in naira terms for every dollar earned, helping sub-Saharan Africa's second-biggest economy to manage a widening deficit.

But the speed of the depreciation in recent days -- around 10 percent since the middle of last week -- has unnerved Nigeria's interbank market, which has long been used to the naira trading in a tight band against the U.S. dollar.

"The central bank sold about $900.13 million to retail banks at a cut-off rate of 130 to the dollar," one dealer said.

Another dealer said the spread had been 130-131.50 naira, compared with a level of around 117 in the middle of last week.

The interbank market has effectively been frozen for three straight days after dollar supply all but dried up as the central bank pushes through the managed devaluation.

Dealers said Friday's dollar sales came too late in the day to kick-start trading and that banks had not been quoting any spreads throughout the day. Many banks bid unsuccessfully at below 130 to the dollar, traders said.

The Nigerian market will be closed on Monday and Tuesday for the Islamic holiday of Eid.

The regulator sold $180 million to one bank on Thursday at a rate of 128 to the dollar, considered too little to calm the market in the face of demand of around $2 billion.

It sold $180 million at its bi-weekly auction on Wednesday at 127-129 to the dollar compared to around 117 a week earlier.

Central Bank Governor Chukwuma Soludo told Reuters late on Wednesday that the regulator was willing to meet all demand for dollars at a market-determined exchange rate.

But the country's banks have appeared reluctant to buy dollars at the rates being offered by the central bank.

They are trying to protect themselves against a weaker naira in the medium-term by been shifting their balance sheets into dollars, further pushing up demand for the greenback and tightening the market, analysts say.

Some analysts have said they believe the central bank may have deliberately been restricting dollar supply to the market in order to flush out speculators and ascertain the true level of underlying demand.

Soludo said on Wednesday that those who had been speculating in the market would be "made to pay a heavy price". (Writing by Nick Tattersall; Editing by Ron Askew)

title: UPDATE 2-Nigeria's  central bank  to act to stabilise naira
text:
(Adds background)

LAGOS, Dec 3 (Reuters) - Nigeria's central bank will intervene in the foreign-exchange market from Thursday to ensure the naira's stability after the local currency fell sharply against the U.S. dollar, Governor Chukwuma Soludo said.

"We are ready to intervene in the market, beginning from tomorrow (Thursday). The central bank will meet all demand at the forex market at the market-determined exchange rate," Soludo told Reuters by telephone.

He said the central bank was ready to buy and sell as necessary.

The naira <NGN=> weakened close to 8 percent to almost 130 to the U.S. dollar on Tuesday as dealers digested the impact of a budget announcement by the president and reacted to what appeared to be a managed depreciation of the local currency.

Banks said no spreads were being quoted on Wednesday on the interbank market as dealers waited for clarity on the central bank's policy and as dollar supply all but dried up.

The central bank allowed the naira, broadly stable against the dollar for months, to depreciate further at its biweekly auction on Wednesday, selling at between 127-129 compared to around 118 on Monday and 116 a week ago.

It sold only $180 million on Wednesday and $100 million on Monday despite demand of about $2 billion, leaving banks scrambling for dollars from other sources.

Soludo blamed the naira's depreciation on speculators.

"Those who have been speculating in the market will be made to pay a heavy price for their actions," he said.

HURT BY DROP IN OIL DEMAND

President Umaru Yar'Adua proposed a 2.87 trillion naira ($24 billion) 2009 budget on Tuesday, a slight increase over actual spending this year despite lower world oil prices, and sought approval to breach a budget deficit target of 3 percent.

That highlighted concern that Nigeria's fiscal position had been impaired significantly by lower world oil demand and the central bank had decided to allow the naira to weaken.

Dealers said dollar demand was being driven by importers before the Christmas trading season as well as by portfolio investors who have been taking money out of Nigeria as the global credit crisis dampens appetite for risk.

It has also been fueled by banks, businesses and individuals -- worried by the long-term impact of falling oil prices on Nigeria's economy -- shifting their balance sheets out of naira into U.S. dollars.

One banking analyst said he thought the central bank may have deliberately restricted dollar supply to the market in order to flush out speculators and ascertain the true level of underlying demand. (Writing by Nick Tattersall; Editing by Jan Paschal)

title: UPDATE 4-Nigeria well placed to weather global crisis -cbank
text:
(Adds comment from head of Oceanic Bank, paragraphs 14-15)

ABUJA, Oct 3 (Reuters) - Nigeria's financial markets are sufficiently liquid, its foreign currency reserves are safe and its banks' balance sheets are strong despite the global credit crisis, central bank governor Chukwuma Soludo said on Friday.

Global market turmoil has led institutional investors to dump perceived risk, dampening enthusiasm for emerging frontier markets like those in sub-Saharan Africa and leading to outflows of foreign capital from countries including Nigeria.

"We now begin to have cross-border contagion," Soludo told a conference in the capital Abuja attended by senior Nigerian bankers, government officials and guest speakers including former U.S. Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers.

"Given the credit crunch in the advanced industrial world, several of the institutional investors from those markets began to pull out of our markets," he said.

The 10 trillion naira ($85 billion) Nigerian Stock Exchange <.LAGLG> has fallen by more than a third since early March to its lowest level in more than a year, although the decline comes against the backdrop of a dismal performance by its peers.

The emerging stocks benchmark <.MSCIEF> dropped to its lowest level since July 2006 on Friday.

But Soludo said the economic fundamentals in the world's eighth biggest oil exporter were sound and said he saw no immediate need for further regulatory intervention.

Nigeria's Monetary Policy Committee decided at an emergency meeting last month to cut its benchmark interest rate to 9.75 percent from 10.25 percent to provide more liquidity.

It also injected about 150 billion naira ($1.3 billion) into sub-Saharan Africa's second biggest economy by reducing the cash reserve requirement to 2 percent from 4 percent.

"We have taken a lot of action in terms of liquidity ... I believe the market is as liquid as it should be at a time like this," he told the meeting.

"Our doors are open, we are free and open to lend to the banks, our discount windows are open, our liquidity ratios are down, our monetary policy rate is down, the minimum cash reserve requirement is down," he said.

STRONG FUNDAMENTALS

What attracted foreign investors to Nigeria in the first place -- the sheer size of its economy meaning its financial markets were relatively liquid -- is also what could shield it from the worst of the global crisis, analysts say.

They say its banks should be well capitalised enough to cope with tightening global credit lines, while in the long term its stock market has enough domestic liquidity to shrug off the departure of some foreign investors.

Cecilia Ibru, head of Oceanic Bank , one of Nigeria's biggest, said foreign credit lines were still open.

"They are still lending to us because we are creating superior value here. We are in a period of growth," she said.

Soludo said Nigerian speculators and regulators had been panicked by the global environment, accelerating the stock market decline. But he told Reuters on the sidelines of the meeting that he believed it was bottoming out.

He said Nigeria's banks had strong balance sheets, were continuing to post profits, and were not under the sort of pressure seen in developed markets such as the United States.

Junior Finance Minister Remi Babalola also told Reuters on Friday that a series of measures to further instil confidence in the Nigerian economy would be announced before the end of the month, including "close collaboration and meetings with banks and companies to ensure that they are not holding risky assets".

President Umaru Yar'Adua painted a rosy economic picture in a state address to mark Independence Day on Wednesday, citing average growth of around 6.9 percent, single-digit inflation and foreign exchange reserves of $63 billion.

Soludo said core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, was running at an acceptable 3.9 percent and said Nigeria's foreign reserves were secure, despite fears they might be at risk from bank failures in the West.

"Our foreign reserves are safe. We have been very prudent in terms of where we put them, the institutions where they are," Soludo said.

Bankers said the market was drained of excess liquidity after investors made purchases at an auction of sovereign bonds on Thursday and importers took advantage of the naira rally to buy more dollars.   

"The initial appreciation of the naira was due to massive dollar sales by some banks that needed naira cash to invest in bonds on behalf of their customers," one dealer said. "Now that the auction is over, the gain is being reversed."   

Nigeria auctioned a total of 42.81 billion naira in 3-year and 10-year sovereign bonds at par with 7.0 percent and 9.35 percent coupon respectively on Thursday, the Debt Management Office said.   

On Wednesday, the naira climbed to its strongest level in five years on a surge in dollar inflows from off-shore interests and some oil multinationals.   

As a consequence of the naira's recent steady rally against the dollar, the central bank has been forced to suspend its twice-weekly forex auction to commercial banks and has indicated it could intervene to slow the naira's rapid appreciation.

text:
LAGOS, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Nigeria's central bank offered $300 million through a special foreign exchange auction on Thursday to satisfy surging demand from the interbank market, bank officials and traders said on Thursday.  

The special auction, the second in two weeks, came a day after the central bank sold $132.80 million at its regular twice-weekly auction to retail banks.  

Dealers said intervention by the central bank, coupled with dollar supply from some oil multinational firms, boosted the value of the naira <NGN=> to 128.40 compared to 128.50 to the dollar on Tuesday on the interbank market.  

Traders said the intervention was probably aimed at mopping up excess cash from the system in anticipation of an inflow of funds from the maturing of 55 billion naira worth of 3-year bonds due to take place on Saturday.  

But one central bank official said it was meant to satisfy a surging appetite for the dollar by dealing banks.  

"Although we have a duty to defend the value of the naira, this time we are satisfying the demand put up by banks at the auction," the official said, asking not to be named.

 The naira strengthened to 128.65 to the dollar at the interbank market on Friday, reversing Thursday's depreciation which saw it drop to 128.80, they added.

 The central bank is the largest supplier of dollars to the foreign exchange market in oil exporter Nigeria, because it is recycling dollar-demoninated oil receipts.

title: Nigerian naira firmer after Cen Bank  intervention .
text:
LAGOS, July 21 (Reuters) - Nigeria's naira currency recovered lost ground against the U.S. dollar in the week to Friday, following spirited moves by the monetary authorities to halt its slide, banking officials said. 

 The officials said the naira exchanged at 106 to the dollar - against 110 last week. 

 "The steps taken so far by the Central bank in the last one week to check the impact of excess liquidity in the system are now having some effects on the value of the naira," said Kunle Alake of Gateway Bank of Nigeria. 

 The naira slumped by nine percent in the past four weeks following a sharp demand for hard currency sending the money market into a turbulence and creating panic among local industries. 

 Industry officials attributed the demand to government budgetary allocations to its ministries and regional governments that had swelled commercial bank liquidity. 

 But the government ordered the ministries and state corporations on Wednesday to move their capital votes from commercial banks to the Central Bank. 

 The Central Bank on the other hand, mopped up over 70 billion naira from the system last week through the auction of government treasury bills. It also called for tenders from banks early this week for the auction of bills worth 121.9 billion naira.

title: FEATURE - New Nigerian ruler faces reform dilemma.
text:
LAGOS, May 24 (Reuters) - The man who did more than anyone to entrench state intervention in Nigeria's economy in the 1970s takes the presidency on Saturday, to the sound of incessant calls for liberal reform. 

 General Olusegun Obasanjo has little choice but to do something radical, given the economic mess he inherits after more than 15 years of corrupt military misrule in the oil-producing country of at least 108 million. 

 But the former army ruler is pulled in two directions. 

 Foreign creditors holding the key to debt relief want the sale of woefully run state enterprises and the scrapping of subsidies as well as independent monitoring of Nigeria's finances. 

 The feeling of many in the presidential camp is that Obasanjo - a down-to-earth farmer who delights in eating with his fingers - has the personal integrity to make sure state intervention is not misdirected this time round. 

 "Obasanjo is a 'government can fix it' kind of guy," said Pat Utomi, Director of the Lagos Business School. 

 "He means well, believes that government can actually fix those problems, but is going to find out quickly that government does not have enough resources to fix them. That will be the telling point," he told Reuters. 

 INDICATORS OF PAIN 

 Low crude prices and a last minute spending splurge by outgoing General Abdulsalami Abubakar's government, have cut foreign reserves to little more than $3 billion from $7 billion in late 1998. 

 Although some foreign exchange went to support the naira, the currency has dropped 20 percent on the open market this year. 

 The stock exchange index is at its lowest since 1995 and down 14 percent this year. 

 "Oil prices have risen since March but even some of the remaining reserves are effectively accounted for by commitments. There is very little to play with," said one official. 

 In a few years, Nigeria may reap a fresh oil and gas bonanza from deep offshore waters far from the volatile Niger Delta region which currently pumps about 1.8 million barrels per day. 

 In the short term, Obasanjo has little more in his favour than foreign goodwill and the fear abroad that economic collapse would end Nigeria's latest attempt at democracy. 

 IMF KEEN TO DEAL 

 Despite Nigeria's failure to meet targets agreed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in January, the Fund hopes to negotiate a medium term programme with the new team to pave the way for short term loans and later debt relief. 

 But the creditors who could reschedule some of an estimated $30 billion debt want to see clear evidence that money is not being stolen or squandered. Some fear Obasanjo feels rescheduling is a right Nigeria has already earned. 

 Britain has promised help only if Nigeria agrees to outside monitors in the finance ministry and central bank. 

 "Once you owe money, you lose an element of sovereignty. But I want to make it clear, that they cannot tell me what to do in Nigeria," Obasanjo told the debt campaign group Jubilee 2000. 

 PRIVATISATION ESSENTIAL FOR SUPPORT 

 Essential for Nigeria to win much outside support is the privatisation of scores of inefficient state enterprises that leave Nigerians short of fuel, power and communications and absorb an estimated $2 billion a year in subsidies. 

 Many of the firms are relics of an era when Obasanjo's last government - like many in Africa - began borrowing for prestige projects and sowed the seeds of later debt crisis. 

 Potentially the biggest privatisation is a sale of part of the state's average 57 percent stake in oil-producing joint ventures. A study by a U.S. bank suggested the sale of only six percent could bring in more than $2 billion. 

 Powerful vested interests have ensured that previous efforts at privatisation have done little more than create new committees and reams of paperwork headed for nowhere but the files. 

 "Privatisation is essential. We're looking at a policy thrust in which we want to free this economy from the constraints that create opportunities for people to collect economic rent," said Utomi. 

 "Perhaps we could still survive without, but life is not about surviving, it's about growth. We've got 65 percent of the population living below the poverty line. I don't know how that can be called surviving." 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1999.

title: FOCUS-Nigeria ministries approve spending spree.
text:
ABUJA, April 30 (Reuters) - Nigerian ministries plan to spend more than 60 billion naira ($630 million) on fresh projects in the dying days of the military administration, officials said on Friday. 

 The new commitments come despite a plunge in foreign reserves to less than $4 billion at the end of March from nearly $7 billion at the end of last year because of increased government spending and low earnings from oil, Nigeria's major export. 

 Government documents obtained by Reuters showed new spending was approved by 10 ministries after a single meeting on April 22. 

 The extra commitments are certain to annoy the incoming administration of President-elect General Olusegun Obasanjo, who is due to take office on May 29. 

 They will also worry donors, who are already concerned at the way foreign reserves have tumbled as the army prepares to bow out after 15 years of corruption-tainted rule in the country of 108 million. 

 "Approval for the spending has been given, although funding has yet to be disbursed," one official told Reuters. 

 Among the funds approved after the April meeting were more than $250 million to improve radar coverage, more than $20 million for an aerial survey of Nigeria's mineral reserves, and money for roads, railways, power lines and new computers. 

 The meeting did not discuss the need for extra spending for Nigeria's involvement in the West African ECOMOG intervention force in Sierra Leone and for strengthening security in the restive oil-rich Niger Delta region. 

 "This spending is the tip of an iceberg," said one analyst with close contacts to General Abdulsalami Abubakar's government. "There will be very little money left to play with by the time Obasanjo takes office." 

 Officials of Obasanjo's Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) reacted cautiously to news of the latest expenditure plans on Friday. 

 "We're not in a position to ascertain such an amount will be spent and are rather hamstrung on making comments," Aniete Okon, PDP spokesman told Reuters. 

 "But if it's true, then it's part of the continuing catalogue of questionable actions taken by the outgoing government," Okon added. 

 Abubakar is hailed at home and abroad for his personal determination to end military rule and embark on liberal economic reforms after assuming power following the death of corrupt dictator Sani Abacha last June. 

 But Abubakar's short-term economic record is clouded at home by severe pressure on the naira currency, which has forced the central bank to tighten liquidity and drive interest rates to 35 percent, the highest in more than a decade. 

 Ending 10 years of sour relations, the International Monetary Fund agreed a staff-monitored programme in January with the understanding that it could lead to a medium-term plan and possible debt relief and concessionary funding. 

 But as well as meeting targets on privatisation and financial stability, Nigeria must also prove it has tried to end its record of massive corruption and of spending on wasteful projects. 

 ($1=95 naira) REUTERS DLM. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1999.

title: Nigerian naira steady on  central bank intervention .
text:
LAGOS, Jan 29 (Reuters) - Central bank intervention has helped stabilise Nigeria's naira, but currency dealers said on Friday there was a limit to how long foreign reserves could last given low oil export prices. 

 On the parallel market the dollar sold for 94 naira, the same level as last week and compared to 97 naira two weeks ago. 

 At the central bank's weekly auction, demand for foreign exchange at 86 naira to the dollar rose to $97 million from $87 million last week - already more than the weekly amount budgeted by the central bank for interventions this year. 

 "The long-term view is one of devaluation. The fundamental is still wrong," said one bank dealer, adding that if the military government kept to its spending plan before stepping down in May, the naira would come under greater pressure. 

 High foreign exchange demand three weeks ago in anticipation of a devaluation fell back after the central bank said it had budgeted $4.4 billion for intervention in 1999 and would defend the naira. 

 But dealers said the central bank was wildly optimistic in its prediction of receipts from private sources of $2.5 billion to fund the foreign exchange market with a further $1.9 billion from government. 

 "The only alternative to devaluation is to use foreign reserves, which is politically popular but unwise in the long term if oil prices stay low," said one banker. 

 ((Paul Okolo, Lagos newsroom +234 1 2630317)).

title: Nigeria  budgets $1.9 bln for  forex intervention .
text:
ABUJA, Jan 5 (Reuters) - Nigeria's military government on Tuesday said it had budgeted $1.9 billion for foreign exchange intervention through the central bank against $2.5 billion the year before. 

 The central bank ran considerably above its 1998 provision for forex intervention to keep the naira currency steady at between 75 and 90 to the dollar despite the weakening of the currency on the parallel market.

title: Nigeria  over budget on exchange  intervention .
text:
LAGOS, July 21 (Reuter) - Nigeria's central bank on Monday said it was over budget on sales of foreign exchange for the first six months of 1997 and had sold about $1.6 billion out of a total $2.72 billion allocated for the year. 

 But in the face of falling demand from customers, despite an appreciating naira currency, bank officials said they believed the target amount need not be breached by the end of the year. 

 Demand, which is used by the central bank to set the rate at which it sells foreign exchange, fell at last week's Thursday sale to $24.6 million from $36.5 million a week earlier. This was in spite of a strengthening of the naira to 83.5 to the dollar from 84 to the dollar the week before. 

 Bankers say that the central bank's demonstrated intention of strengthening the naira over recent weeks has helped dampen demand, as they wait to see at what level the currency will be allowed to settle. 

 But they say the main reason for low demand is that business has been badly hit by recession. 

 The recession is blamed by manufacturers and importers on government's reluctance to spend proceeds of crude oil exports locally out of fear of inflation and of weakening the naira. 

 Apparent victory in the war on inflation and the stabilisation of the naira are seen by supporters of military ruler General Sani Abacha as the prizes of tight fiscal policies since he took power in the economic and political chaos after the annulment of 1993 elections.

title: Nigeria  moves to weekly  forex intervention .
text:
LAGOS, May 22 (Reuter) - Nigeria changed to weekly from monthly intervention on its foreign exchange markets on Wednesday, the central bank said. 

 The Central Bank of Nigeria said the decision to intervene weekly on the Autonomous Foreign Exchange market points to currency stability and could eventually strengthen the naira. 

 "It should remove speculative demand, and when there is no pressure to buy more than may be needed, it will further stabilise the naira," central bank spokesman Tony Ede told Reuters. 

 "Eventually we would like to see the currency appreciate." 

 A rate of 82.50 naira has been proposed to the 77 commercial and merchant banks bidding for foreign currency on Wednesday. 

 The central bank has not revealed the amount it will sell. 

 But some bankers worried whether the central bank would be able to meet weekly requirements. 

 "If it removes speculative demand it removes unnecessarily inflated rates and also the need to borrow large sums of money monthly, so we save on the cost of borrowing," said one banker. 

 "But I am not convinced the central bank has the ability to fund the operation on a weekly basis," he added. 

 The central bank is confident it can meet the demand. 

 "We felt it is not necessary to state the amount we are offering because we have been able to meet demand since last year on the monthly basis and we are sure we will be able to supply whatever is required," said Ede. 

 Over the past year the naira has attained a stability unprecedented in Nigeria's recent past, hovering around 80 to 85 naira to the dollar. 

 This has helped to bring down inflation. Some estimates for annual inflation have gone from above 80 percent a year ago to less than 50 percent now. 

 Many economic operators hope intervention eventually strengthens the naira, a declared aim of the central bank. 

 "We asked for more regular intervention but one would want to be sure that the amount on offer will be at least the same as it is now on the monthly basis," director-general of the Manuafacturers Association of Nigeria, Uzor Ekeke said. 

 "Most of our members are reliant on imports for the local market, exports are small, so if the naira strengthened it would definitely be good for us," he added. 

 Ede said he could not disclose the rate which the central bank had in mind as a target value for the currency. 

 "We are still going to follow the market," he said. 

 "I think it would be good to see the interventions eventually leading to a rate of around 60 naira to the dollar," said one banker.

title: Nigeria Central Bank  to  intervene  in  forex  market.
text:
LAGOS, Nov 16 (Reuter) - Nigeria's Central Bank said it would intervene via auction in the foreign exchange market on Monday to shore up the naira currency. 

 It said in a statement that $100 million would be offered for sale at a rate of 85 naira to the dollar, and it listed about 70 banks selected to participate in the periodic auction. 

 The naira fell on Thursday to its lowest level this year on fears the hanging of nine rights activists last week will lead to international economic pressure on the country, dealers said. 

 Dealers said the naira had fallen to between 90 and 92 to the dollar in the autonomous market compared to the 80-85 level where it had been trading for most of the year. 

 "The naira is responding to the situation in the country," said foreign exchange bureau operator Taiye Abiodun. 

 Nigeria has come under international condemnation since last Friday when the nine members of the Movement for the Survival of Ogoni Peoples (MOSOP), including its president, writer Ken Saro-Wiwa, were hanged. 

 Dozens of ambassadors were swiftly recalled from Lagos  and economic sanctions against the country were being discussed by the European Union. 

 Monday's auction of foreign exchange willl be the fourth by the Central Bank this year.

title: Nigeria still hopeful of early deal with IMF.
text:
ABUJA, May 22 (Reuter) - Nigeria will later this week begin talks with the IMF which it hopes will produce an early accord to pave way for negotiations with mainly western creditors for debt relief. 

 Nigeria's finance minister Anthony Ani said his government was still aiming to reach an agreement with the IMF and the World Bank on a "home grown" Medium Term Economic Adjustment Programme by the start of the third quarter of 1995. 

 "We are still very optimistic because we are on course," he told Reuters in an interview on Monday. 

 Ani said he was confident that policy differences between Nigeria and the IMF could be iron out at the talks. 

 The start of the talks with a visiting IMF team has been shifted from Monday to May 27 because of the annual meeting of the African Development Bank in Abuja this week. 

 In its 1995 budget Nigeria's military government announced measures that took the country back along the path of free market reforms after a year of turning its back on IMF-backed reforms started by the previous administration in 1986. 

 International finance agencies have commended aspects of the 1995 budget, including the re-introduction of an autonomous foreign exchange market and the removal of laws that restricted inflow of foreign investment. 

 But they say the government needs to further liberalise the economy, including abolishing the official exchange rate of 22 naira to the dollar, a fraction of rates of about 83.50 naira to the dollar available in the autonomous market. 

 They also oppose the retention of a 21 percent ceiling on interest rates and apparent moves to take over privatised banks. 

 Ani said the official exchange rate exists only for internal accounting purposes and that the effective rate in the economy was that of the autonomous market. 

 He said the government aims for a unified rate and hoped to reach an agreement with IMF on a time-table for achieving this. 

 "We hope to come to an agreement when this will cease. We are not going to have two rates for ever. We expect them to merge between now and the next 18 months," he said. 

 Ani said the government was looking at ways to make the central bank discount rate the focus of bank interest rates. 

 He added that the government would not allow a return to the 1993 situation when interest rates topped 100 percent. 

 "We cannot allow a situation where banks move interest rates so that they adversely affect manufacturers and the economy." 

 Ani said the government was still committed to the policy of privatisation began by the previous military administration in 1988 and suspended in January this year by the present regime. 

 "We are not going back on the privatisation policies. Government is committed to privatisation," he said. 

 He said government plans to re-establish its presence in the country's four biggest banks, privatised between 1992 and 1993, does not involve re-nationalisation. 

 He said the decision to intervene in the First Bank of Nigeria, Union Bank, United Bank for Africa and Afribank was to prevent them being taken over by some people and then made distressed. He said 49 out of Nigeria 120 banks are distressed. 

 "There are maneuvers now by certain individuals to hijack and take over the four banks," he said. 

 Ani said the operations of the four banks were too crucial to the economy for the government to allow them to be taken over by people who might run them to the ground. 

 He stressed that the state will not take over shares already issued or nationalise holdings of foreign shareholders. 

 The government is believed to be planning to buy unissued shares in these banks and raise their capital. 

 Ani said the government's Medium Term Adjustment Programme is an update of the programme worked out in 1993 by the then head of the Transitional Council, businessman Ernest Shonekan. 

 That three-year programme, which was never implemented, was was geared to achieving a 5.3 percent average real GDP annual growth rate, cut inflation to five percent, reduce fiscal deficit as a percentage of GDP to 3.3 percent.

title: Nigeria  central bank  cautious on  forex  policy.
text:
LAGOS, Feb 16 (Reuter) - The central bank (CBN) will not intervene in Nigeria's newly legalised autonomous foreign exchange market until banks raise their quotes for official funds, the bank's spokesman said on Thursday. 

 "The days of cheap foreign exchange are over. There is no more subsidised forex," CBN spokesman Tony Ede told Reuters. 

 He said daily exchange rates quoted by banks to the CBN have not so far reflected the state of the market. 

 "The rates they are quoting for the dollar are too low. They are not the same rates as we know the banks are actually selling the currency,"  he said. 

 He did not say what rates banks have quoted the CBN. 

 Banks on Thursday quoted to the public a dollar selling rate of between 78 and 82 naira. 

 The dollar sold for about 105 naira in November before falling partly on anticipation of the announcment of the 1995 government budget. 

 The government, under pressure from local private sector groups and foreign creditors, in mid-January legalised the autonomous market after a year of imposing an officially set and highly subsidised fixed exchange rate regime. 

 Paul Ogwuma, CBN governor, said at a luncheon on Thursday Nigeria had become over-dependent on imported raw materials and finished goods. 

 "This largely stems from the past misalignment of the naira exchange rate - which subsidised the consumption of foreign goods and services to the disadvantage of domestic production. 

 "We are indeed hopeful that the new exchange rate policy, if sustained, shall compel the economy to look inwards for a change," he said. 

 The CBN has stopped its fortnightly forex sales to the public, saying it would intervene when it deems it necessary. 

 The autonomous market has not fully taken off partly because banks and their clients are waiting for the CBN to intervene and inject scarce hard currency into the system. 

 Many people believe the CBN will inject money into the system at rates below those of the free market. 

 It appears the central bank is also waiting for the market to come to terms with a CBN that seems committed to promoting free market forces after years of artificially propping up the naira. 

 "We are waiting for them to understand the system. The market has not come to grips yet with the current reality. We are not getting the right signals," Ede said. 

 Under the new system the CBN when it intervenes will sell foreign exchange directly to end users through selected banks. 

 Managers at Nigeria's 116 commercial and merchant banks have been anxious to know what criteria the CBN will use to select the banks. 

 With the CBN controlling the bulk of the hard currency that is likely to be traded in the autonomous market, no bank wants to be left out of its list. 

 Ede said banks able to buy and sell at the highest rates stood the best chance. 

 "We know the active banks in the market. We will look at their rates and sell through them to end users at the highest rates quoted by these banks," he said. 

 (c) Reuters Limited 1995

title: Nigeria  forex  market slow, awaits  central bank  move.
text:
LAGOS, Feb 16 (Reuter) - Trading remains slow in Nigeria's newly legalised autonomous foreign exchange market as banks and their clients wait for the central bank to make its first intervention and inject scarce funds into the system. 

 "We don't have funds to sell nor do we have buyers. People are anticipating a CBN (Central Bank of Nigeria) intervention anytime from now," a dealer in one of Nigeria's leading commercial banks said. 

 The naira now stands at about 82 to the dollar, barely changed from the week's start. 

 "There has been little movement in the market because people are still waiting to see how the new system works," a forex dealer at another Lagos-based commercial bank said. 

 Many exporters remain reluctant to repatriate their hard currency proceeds through authorised banks because they are either awaiting better exchange rates or doubt the durability of the military government's new liberalisation move, bankers said. 

 The government, under pressure from local private sector groups and foreign creditors, legalised the autonomous market in mid-January after a year of imposing an officially set and highly subsidised fixed exchange rate regime. 

 Under the new system, banks and exchange bureaux are free to set market-determined rates. 

 The CBN has stopped its fortnightly forex sales to the public, saying it would intervene when it deemed necessary. 

 The CBN, whose funds account for the bulk of domestic foreign exchange supplies, has not had a formal sale since mid-December, though it has sold funds to some corporations. 

 Many manufacturers and other importers are waiting for Central Bank intervention before buying foreign exchange, assuming a CBN sale would strengthen the naira. 

 Some private sector groups have criticised the central bank for not pumping foreign exchange into the import-dependent economy until now. "The CBN is just standing by watching. It should intervene now," Uzor Okeke, director-general of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN) told Reuters. 

 He said the intervention should aim to strengthen the naira so that local production costs do not rise. 

 Uncertainty in the financial sector and delays in the issue of new import tariffs were hampering productive activity, Okeke said. "Companies haven't started importing. They are still using stocks which will run out.It is a dangerous situation," he said.

title: Nigeria's  forex  decision seen ruining some banks.
text:
LAGOS, Feb 10 (Reuter) - The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) said on Friday it would sell hard currency directly to end users through selected banks when it intervenes in Nigeria's newly legalised autonomous foreign exchange market. 

 The CBN, issuing guidelines on mechanisms of a liberalised foreign exchange market announced by the government last month, said the selected banks may charge transaction fees and commissions. 

 Bankers in Lagos, Nigeria's financial hub, said the decision to use only some banks to sell scarce hard currency was likely to lead to the collapse of some of the other banks. 

 "If they insist on selling foreign exchange only through some banks we will surely see many bank failures this year," said a forex dealer in one of the country's top three banks. 

 "There is going to be a massive movement of naira out of banks that don't qualify to sell government funds," he said. 

 Banks are anxious to be among those chosen by the CBN beause official funds, mainly oil export earnings, account for the bulk of money likely to be traded in the market. 

 "Right now every bank wants to know what criteria CBN will use to select the banks it will do business with," said a Lagos-based commercial banker. "There is going to be a mad rush to be one of the chosen ones." 

Foreign exchange dealing is the main source of profit for banks in Nigeria's import-dependent economy. 

 Bankers said the CBN may decide not to sell foreign exchange through financially-distressed banks. 

 CBN officials say 36 out of Nigeria's 116 commercial and merchant banks are distressed but decline to name them. 

 Last year the CBN liquidated four banks because their financial situation were considered irreparable. 

 "The new foreign exchange system will quicken the death of distressed banks," said a manager at a merchant bank. 

 The CBN said it would intervene in the autonomous forex market when it deems necessary, "giving only short notice of such intervention". It said it would buy at the current autonomous selling rate in the market. 

 The dollar sold for as high as 82 naira on Friday compared to 78 naira on Monday. 

 Volume of transactions in the autonomous market remains small as people wait for the new system to show how it works and for the CBN to pump funds into the market. 

 All individuals, private sector operators and state-run companies operating on a commercial basis must now buy their foreign exchange from the autonomous market. 

 The government still maintains an official exchange rate of 22 naira to the dollar but that rate applies only to certain government transactions. 

 Private sector groups have said the two-tier system is open to abuse as officials with access to subsidised hard currency may be tempted to divert to the autonomous market.

title: Nigeria's  forex  move may ruin some banks - bankers.
text:
LAGOS, Feb 10 (Reuter) - The central bank's decision to sell scarce foreign exchange to the public through selected banks is likely to lead to the collapse of some of Nigeria's banks who are not chosen, bankers said. 

 "If they insist on selling foreign exchange only through some banks we will surely see many bank failures this year," said a forex dealer in one of the country's top three banks. 

 The central bank (CBN) said in guidelines issued on Friday that it would sell hard currency directly to end users through selected banks when it intervenes in the newly legalised autonomous foreign exchange market. 

 It said banks not chosen could still take part in the autonomous market which also gets funds from the private sector. 

 With official funds accounting for the bulk of money likely to be traded in the market, banks are anxious to be among those chosen by the CBN. 

 "Right now every bank wants to know what criteria CBN will use to select the banks it will do business with," said a Lagos-based commercial banker. "There is going to be a mad rush to be one of the chosen ones," he added. 

Foreign exchange dealing is the main business of banks in this import-dependent economy. 

 "There is going to be a massive movement of naira out of banks that don't qualify to sell government funds," said the forex dealer. 

 Bankers say the CBN may decide not to sell foreign exchange through financially-distressed banks. 

 CBN officials say 36 out of Nigeria's 116 commercial and merchant banks are distressed but decline to name them. 

 Last year the CBN liquidated four banks because their financial situation were considered irreparable. 

 "The new foreign exchange system will quicken the death of distressed banks," said a manager with a merchant bank. 

 The CBN guidelines, which had been anxiously awaited by banks, said central bank intervention in the autonomous forex market shall be "when considered necessary giving only short notice of such intervention." 

 "The Central Bank of Nigeria shall sell foreign exchange at the current autonomous selling rate in the market," it said.

title: Nigerian banks to sell  forex  directly to end users.
text:
LAGOS, Feb 10 (Reuter) - The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) said it will sell hard currency directly to end users when it intervenes in the newly legalised autonomous foreign exchange market. 

 It said in guidelines on the liberalised foreign exchange market announced by the government last month that it would sell funds to end users through selected banks who may charge transaction charges and commission but not a spread. 

 The guidelines did not say what criteria would be used to select the banks. 

 Nigeria's 116 commercial and merchant banks have anxiously waited for the CBN to spell out how it planned to intervene in the autonomous market. 

 The CBN said the intervention shall be "when considered necessary giving only short notice of such intervention." 

 "The Central Bank of Nigeria shall sell foreign exchange at the current autonomous selling rate in the market," it said. 

 The CBN earlier this week issued and later withdrew guidelines which said it would sell forex at the highest interbank rates. 

 Friday's guidelines said banks must submit to CBN summaries of their client's applications for foreign exchange within 48 hours from the time of notification of intervention by the CBN.

title: Nigeria aims to make naira convertible  currency .
text:
LAGOS, Jan 24 (Reuter) - The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) said it was working towards making the naira a convertible currency. 

 "The major policy goal for 1995 is the deliberate build-up and strengthening of external reserves to enhance confidence in the Nigerian economy, strengthen the naira and pave the way for its ultimate convertibility," CBN governor Paul Ogwuma told a rare news conference in Lagos. 

 Nigeria's external reserves last July stood at $669 million, barely enough to pay for six weeks worth of imports. The government on January 14 legalised the foreign exchange market in a move back to free market reforms abandoned a year ago. 

 Ogwuma said the government's 1994 policy of fixing the exchange rate at 22 naira to the dollar, a fraction of rates in the parallel market, had not worked. 

 "In the area of foreign exchange management, lessons of experience have clearly shown that the regime of fixed exchange rates that was pursued in 1994 did not achieve the intended policy objectives," he said. 

 The government fixed the exchange rate in a bid to strengthen the naira which in 1985 was worth more than a dollar. 

 Under the new system the interbank market is free to operate rates mutually agreed between buyers and sellers. 

 The central bank has stopped its fortnightly forex sales and says it will instead intervene periodically in the autonomous market by selling and buying foreign exchange at market rates. 

 There has been few transactions in the autonomous market as banks wait for the CBN to sell them scarce hard currency. 

 Official foreign exchange earnings, mainly from crude oil exports, account for the bulk of Nigeria's hard currency inflow. 

 Ogwuma said the CBN would intervene in the autonomous market having conducted a survey of banks' buying and selling rates as well as their foreign exchange requirements. The CBN did not expect demand for its hard currency to be as high as it was last year when it sold funds at highly subsidised official rates. 

 The increased cost of hard currency will force importers to seek local substitutes for imported production inputs, he said. 

 "The demand for foreign exchange is well within our means to meet," he said. "Most of the people who demanded dollars last year are going to be looking inwards this year," he said. 

 The government still maintains an official exchange rate of 22 naira to the dollar, but that rate applies to a limited number of government transactions. 

 All individuals, private sector operators and government parastatals run on commercial basis must buy their foreign exchange from the autonomous market where the dollar now sells at well above 70 naira. 

 Bankers say the two-tier foreign exchange system is open to abuse as officials with access to subsidised hard currency may be tempted to divert to to the autonomous market. 

 Ogwuma said the government would take steps to prevent the occurance of this practice reputed to have made some well placed people rich in the past. 

 "What the government is going to do is to ensure there is no round-tripping," he said.
